title: DOL Suspends New PERM Green Card Filings by Cognizant, Cloudera
excerpt: The Labor Department's inspector general froze new permanent labor certification filings at the two tech firms amid a fraud probe — stalling green card sponsorships for thousands of H-1B workers, with no charges yet announced.
body:
• The U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General announced on September 8, 2026, that new PERM labor certification filings by Cognizant Technology Solutions and Cloudera have been suspended while investigators examine alleged fraud and abuse in employment-based immigration programs.
  • The suspension blocks only new permanent labor certification filings — the first step toward sponsoring a worker for a green card. It does not revoke existing PERM approvals or H-1B petitions.
  • No criminal charges have been announced and the department has not disclosed the specific allegations against either company; both moves were announced on social media by Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, not in a formal press release.
  • For the thousands of Indian professionals on H-1B visas at these firms, the freeze stalls new green card sponsorships — and the six-year H-1B extensions that depend on pending PERM or approved I-140 petitions.

The Department of Labor has suspended the ability of two major tech employers — Cognizant Technology Solutions and Cloudera — to file new permanent labor certification (PERM) applications, the first step toward sponsoring foreign workers for U.S. green cards. The move, announced September 8 by Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, puts the India-founded IT services giant and the Santa Clara-based data and AI company at the center of a widening investigation into alleged fraud and abuse in employment-based immigration programs.

D'Esposito posted the news directly on social media rather than through a formal press release. "Threats to American workers will NOT be tolerated," he wrote, adding that investigators were working with the Labor Department and the White House Fraud Task Force to examine the allegations, according to coverage in TR Immigration. About an hour after announcing the Cognizant suspension, he announced the same measure against Cloudera.

What was actually suspended — and what was not

PERM — the Program Electronic Review Management system — is the Labor Department's permanent labor certification process, generally the mandatory first step before an employer can sponsor a foreign worker for an employment-based green card. Employers must run a prescribed recruitment process and certify that no qualified U.S. worker is available and that the hire will not depress wages or working conditions. The suspension blocks only new PERM filings from the two companies; it does not touch existing approvals or H-1B petitions, which USCIS handles separately. The action does not establish that either company committed fraud — no charges have been announced, no specific allegations have been disclosed, and neither company had publicly responded as of publication.

A separate enforcement track against Cloudera

For Cloudera, the new suspension lands on top of an existing enforcement action. In May 2026, the Labor Department's Employment and Training Administration announced it had suspended processing of all permanent labor certification applications filed by or on behalf of Cloudera for 180 days, following allegations that the company violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by unlawfully discriminating against American workers in favor of foreign labor.

The DOJ's Civil Rights Division alleged Cloudera had engineered a "nonfunctional" recruitment process that blocked qualified U.S. workers from applying for high-paying roles while certifying that none were available. In April 2026, the DOJ sued the company before its Office of the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer.

For Cognizant, the timing is striking. The suspension came just a day after the company announced plans to hire 1,500 U.S. college graduates and grow its "Frontier" certified engineering and business operator workforce to 15,000 people, and said it had joined RAISE US, a coalition focused on moving American workers into AI-related jobs. Department of Labor data show the company's use of the H-1B program has declined in recent years: it filed 3,436 labor condition applications in 2025, down from 10,189 in 2018, according to TR Immigration.

Impact on Indian professionals

The consequences land most directly on the H-1B workers at both companies and their families — many of them Indian nationals who own homes, have U.S.-citizen children in school, and hold spouses on H-4 work authorization tied to approved I-140 petitions. Many are counting on H-1B extensions beyond the normal six-year limit, which depend on a pending PERM case or an approved I-140 — exactly the pipeline the suspension freezes. Immigration attorney Vasanth Vaidyanathan also warned that mid-sized companies sponsoring H-1B and PERM workers should be reviewing their recruitment documentation and audit files now, to prove they can withstand similar scrutiny.

What's next

The Labor Department has not said when the suspensions might lift, and the DOJ investigation will determine whether further action follows. Anyone with a pending case at either company should confirm exactly where their PERM, I-140, or H-1B extension stands with their immigration attorney — the practical effect will be felt long before any investigation concludes.
